replacement: 11. I must say a discouraging word here about the recent attempts to base the origin of justice on something quite different, namely resentment. Let me whisper in the psychologists' ear, if they want to study revenge itself up close: this plant flourishes loveliest today among Anarchists and anti-Semites. It is a hidden flower, as it has always been, like the violet, though, to be sure, with another perfume. Like must come from like, so we should not be surprised to find in just such circles the birth of efforts (it is their old birthplace; compare above, First Essay, paragraph 14) to sanctify revenge under the name of justice, as though Justice were at bottom only a development of the consciousness of injury. By rehabilitating revenge in this way, they hope to reinstate all the reactive emotions generally and collectively. That last point is the one I object to least. Seen from the standpoint of the whole problem of biology (from which the value of these emotions has until now been underestimated), it even seems meritorious. What I alone want to point out is that this new nuance of scientific equity (which works for the benefit of hate, envy, mistrust, jealousy, suspicion, rancor, revenge) grows out of the spirit of revenge itself. This scientific "equity" breaks off at once, and makes way for the accents of deadly enmity and prejudice, whenever another group of emotions appears. In my opinion these emotions have a much higher biological value than the reactions, and so have a paramount claim to the valuation and appreciation of science: I mean the really active emotions, such as personal and material ambition, and so forth. (E. Dühring, Value of Life; Course of Philosophy, and passim.) That is enough against this tendency in general. As for Dühring's particular maxim, that the home of Justice lies in the sphere of the reactive feelings, our love of truth forces us to turn his own proposition sharply around and set against it this other: the last sphere conquered by the spirit of justice is the sphere of the feeling of reaction! Suppose the just man really stays just even toward the person who injures him (and is not merely cold, moderate, reserved, indifferent: being just is always a positive state). Suppose that, despite the strong provocation of personal insult, contempt and calumny, the lofty, clear objectivity of the just and judging eye (whose glance is as profound as it is gentle) remains untroubled. Why, then we have a piece of perfection, a past master of the world; but it would not be wise to expect such a thing, and at any rate it should not be too easily believed. Speaking generally, there is no doubt that even the justest individual needs only a small dose of hostility, malice or innuendo to send the blood to his head and drive the fairness out. The active, attacking, aggressive man is always a hundred degrees nearer to justice than the man who merely reacts. He certainly has no need to use the tactics the reacting man must use, of falsifying and biasing his valuation of his object. For this very reason the aggressive man has at all times had the stronger, bolder, more aristocratic and also freer outlook, and the better conscience. On the other hand, we already suspect who has the invention of the "bad conscience" on his own conscience: the resentful man! Finally, let man look at himself in history. Where has the whole administration of law, the real need of law, had its earthly home until now? Perhaps with the reacting man? Not for a minute. Rather with the active, strong, spontaneous, aggressive man? I deliberately defy the agitator I mentioned (who himself makes this self-confession, "the creed of revenge has run through all my works and endeavors like the red thread of Justice"), and I say that, judged historically, law on earth is the very war against the reactive feelings. It is a war waged on them by the powers of activity and aggression, which spend part of their strength on damming and holding within bounds this effervescence of hysterical reactivity, and on forcing it into some compromise. Wherever justice is practiced and maintained, we can see the stronger power looking for weapons to end the senseless fury of resentment among the weaker powers beneath it (whether groups or individuals). It does this partly by pulling the victim of resentment out of the clutches of revenge, partly by putting a campaign of its own against the enemies of peace and order in the place of revenge, partly by finding, suggesting and sometimes enforcing settlements, and partly by fixing standard equivalents for injuries, to which resentment is from then on finally referred. The most drastic step the supreme power takes against the preponderance of spite and vindictiveness, and it takes it as soon as it is strong enough, is to found law: it declares imperatively what in its eyes counts as just and lawful and what as unjust and unlawful. Once law is founded, the supreme power treats the aggressive and arbitrary acts of individuals, or of whole groups, as violations of law and as revolt against itself. That draws its subjects' feelings away from the immediate injury such a violation causes, and so in the end it achieves the very opposite of what revenge always wants, since revenge sees and recognizes only the standpoint of the injured party. From then on the eye is trained toward an ever more impersonal valuation of the deed, even the eye of the injured party himself (though that comes last of all, as I remarked before). On this principle "right" and "wrong" first arise after the foundation of law (and not, as Dühring maintains, only after the act of violation). To speak of intrinsic right and intrinsic wrong is absolute nonsense. An injury, an oppression, an exploitation, an annihilation cannot be intrinsically wrong, because life is essentially (that is, in its cardinal functions) something that works by injuring, oppressing, exploiting and annihilating, and cannot be conceived at all without this character. I must make a still more serious confession. From the most advanced biological standpoint, conditions of legality can only be exceptional conditions. They are partial restrictions of the real life-will, which aims at power, and they are subordinate to that life-will's general end as particular means, that is, as means of creating larger units of strength. Imagine a legal organization conceived as sovereign and universal, not as a weapon in the fight between complexes of power but as a weapon against fighting, something in the style of Dühring's communistic model in which every will is treated as equal to every other will. It would be a principle hostile to life, a destroyer and dissolver of man, an outrage on the future of man, a symptom of fatigue, a secret path to Nothingness. —

replacement: 13. Back to our subject, punishment. We must draw a double distinction. On one side is the relatively permanent element: the custom, the act, the "drama," a certain rigid sequence of procedures. On the other is the fluid element: the meaning, the end, the expectation that goes with carrying out such procedures. Here we at once assume, per analogiam (following the theory of the historical method developed above), that the procedure itself is older and earlier than its use for punishment. That use was introduced and read into the procedure (which had existed for a long time but was employed with another meaning). In short, the case is different from what our naïf genealogists of morals and of law have supposed until now. They thought the procedure was invented for the purpose of punishment, just as they had earlier thought the hand was invented for the purpose of grasping. Now the other element in punishment, the fluid one, its meaning. At a very late stage of civilization (for instance in contemporary Europe), the idea of punishment no longer shows just one meaning but a whole synthesis "of meanings." The past history of punishment in general, the history of its use for the most diverse ends, finally crystallizes into a kind of unity that is hard to break down into its parts, and that, it must be stressed, absolutely defies definition. (Today it is impossible to say definitely why people punish at all. Every idea in which a whole process is promiscuously summed up eludes definition; only what has no history can be defined.) At an earlier stage, on the contrary, that synthesis of meanings looks much less rigid and much more elastic. We can see how, in each individual case, the elements of the synthesis change their value and their position, so that now one element stands out and dominates the rest, now another; nay, in certain cases one element (perhaps the end of deterrence) seems to wipe out all the others. At any rate, to give some idea of how uncertain, supplementary and accidental the meaning of punishment is, and of how one identical procedure can be used and adapted for the most diametrically opposed objects, I will set down here a scheme that has suggested itself to me, itself based on comparatively small and accidental material. — Punishment as making the criminal harmless and unable to do further injury. — Punishment as compensation to the injured party for the injury sustained, in any form whatsoever (including the form of sentimental compensation). — Punishment as the isolation of whatever disturbs the equilibrium, in order to stop the disturbance from spreading further. — Punishment as a means of inspiring fear of those who determine and carry out the punishment. — Punishment as a kind of compensation for advantages the wrong-doer has enjoyed until then (for example, when he is put to work as a slave in the mines). — Punishment as the elimination of an element of decay (sometimes of a whole branch, as under the Chinese laws, and so as a means of purifying the race or preserving a social type). — Punishment as a festival, as the violent oppression and humiliation of an enemy who has at last been subdued. — Punishment as a mnemonic, whether for the man who suffers it (the so-called "correction") or for those who witness it being carried out. Punishment as the payment of a fee stipulated by the power that protects the evil-doer from the excesses of revenge. — Punishment as a compromise with the natural phenomenon of revenge, in so far as the stronger races still maintain revenge and claim it as a privilege. — Punishment as a declaration and measure of war against an enemy of peace, of law, of order, of authority. Society fights him with the weapons war provides, as a spirit dangerous to the community, as a breaker of the contract on which the community is based, as a rebel, a traitor and a breaker of the peace.

14. This list is certainly not complete; punishment, obviously, is overloaded with utilities of every kind. That makes it all the more permissible to remove one supposed utility, which passes, at any rate in the popular mind, for the most essential of all. It is just this utility that still gives the strongest support to the faith in punishment, a faith that is tottering today for many reasons. Punishment is supposed to be valuable because it awakens in the guilty the consciousness of guilt. In punishment people look for the proper instrumentum of that psychic reaction known as the "bad conscience," "remorse." But this theory violates reality and psychology even as applied to the present; how much worse when it is applied to the longest period of man's history, his primitive history! Genuine remorse is certainly extremely rare among wrong-doers and the victims of punishment. Prisons and houses of correction are not the soil in which this worm of remorse likes best to breed. All conscientious observers agree on this, and in many cases they reach such a judgment only reluctantly and against their own wishes. Generally speaking, punishment hardens and numbs, it concentrates, it sharpens the consciousness of alienation, it strengthens the power of resistance. Sometimes it breaks a man's energy and brings about a piteous prostration and abjectness. That result is certainly even less salutary than the average effect of punishment, which is a harsh and sinister doggedness. Thinking of those prehistoric millennia, we must conclude without hesitation that punishment, more than anything, held back the development of the consciousness of guilt, at any rate in the victims of the punishing power. In particular, let us not underestimate how far the sight of the judicial and executive procedure itself keeps the wrong-doer from feeling that his deed, the character of his act, is intrinsically reprehensible. He sees the same kind of acts clearly practiced in the service of justice, then called good, and practiced with a good conscience: espionage, trickery, bribery, trapping, the whole intriguing and insidious art of the policeman and the informer. He sees the whole system, in fact, that appears in the various kinds of punishment (a system excused not by passion but based on principle), of robbing, oppressing, insulting, imprisoning, racking, murdering. And he sees his judges treat all this not as acts deserving censure and condemnation in themselves, but only in a particular context and application. The "bad conscience," that most sinister and interesting plant of our earthly vegetation, did not grow in this soil. In fact, for a very long period, the man who judged and punished had no idea at all that he was dealing with a "guilty man." He was dealing merely with the author of an injury, an irresponsible piece of fate. And the man on whom the punishment then fell like a piece of fate felt no more "inner pain" than he would feel at the sudden approach of some unforeseen event, some terrible natural catastrophe, a rushing, crushing avalanche against which there is no resistance.

replacement: 15. This truth dawned insidiously on Spinoza (to the disgust of his commentators, who, like Kuno Fischer, for instance, go to endless trouble to misunderstand him on this point). One afternoon, as he sat raking up who knows what memory, he asked himself what was really left for him personally of the celebrated morsus conscientiæ. Here was a man who had relegated "good and evil" to the sphere of human imagination, and who indignantly defended the honor of his "free" God against the blasphemers who claimed that God did everything sub ratione boni ("but this was tantamount to subordinating God to fate, and would really be the greatest of all absurdities"). For Spinoza the world had gone back to that innocence in which it lay before the bad conscience was discovered. So what had become of the morsus conscientiæ? "The antithesis of gaudium," he said at last to himself: "A sadness accompanied by the recollection of a past event which has turned out contrary to all expectation" (Eth. III., Propos. XVIII. Schol. i. ii.). For thousands of years, evil-doers overtaken by punishment have felt about their "offence" exactly as Spinoza did: "here is something which went wrong contrary to my anticipation," not "I ought not to have done this." They submitted to punishment as one submits to a disease, a misfortune or death, with that stubborn, resigned fatalism that even now gives the Russians, for instance, an advantage over us Westerners in managing life. If actions were criticized at that period, the criterion was prudence. What punishment unquestionably achieves is chiefly a sharper sense of prudence, a longer memory, a will to be more cautious, suspicious and secretive from now on, a recognition that many things are unquestionably beyond one's capacity, and a kind of improvement in self-criticism. In man and beast alike, the broad results that punishment can obtain are increased fear, a sharper sense of cunning, and mastery of the desires. So punishment tames man, but does not make him "better"; it would be more correct even to go so far as to assert the contrary ("Injury makes a man cunning," says a popular proverb: so far as it makes him cunning, it makes him also bad. Fortunately, it often enough makes him stupid).
